Mature individuals of the Doubleline eelpout (Lycodes eudipleurostictus) attain a maximum recorded total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], which positions this species among the medium-sized members of its genus. Reaching such an ultimate length appears to require sustained growth over many years in the cold waters of the northern Pacific, where this benthic zoarcid is typically encountered on muddy substrates at depths exceeding one hundred meters. Field surveys indicate that the species exhibits a relatively slow growth trajectory, consistent with the low metabolic rates common among deep-dwelling fishes. The largest specimens are usually gravid females captured during late winter trawls, suggesting that somatic growth continues well after the onset of reproductive activity. In comparison with the congeneric species Lycodes raridens, which rarely surpasses 35 centimeters in total length, this eelpout achieves a notably larger asymptotic body size that may confer advantages in fecundity and competitive dominance in resource-limited environments.

Embryonic development in Lycodes eudipleurostictus has been examined under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the stable thermal regime of its deep-sea habitat, with incubations maintained at a constant temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]. Under these conditions, the age at birth occurs at approximately 155 days [ab = approximately 155 days], an extended incubation period that reflects the slow pace of physiological processes in this cold-adapted teleost at a temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae are relatively small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0871 grams [Wwb = 0.0871 grams], a mass derived from the average egg diameter of 5.5 millimeters typical of the species. This modest neonatal mass is consistent with the production of numerous small offspring, a reproductive strategy common among deep-sea fishes that face high larval mortality. The initial dependence on endogenous yolk reserves persists for several weeks, during which the prolarvae remain largely motionless near the bottom, conserving energy before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Under the stable cold regime characteristic of its habitat (3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]), sexual maturation in this species occurs after an extended juvenile phase, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 3 years [tp = 3 years]. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 114.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 114.6 grams], and the total length at puberty measures about 19.5 centimeters [Lp = about 19.5 centimeters]. These values indicate that reproductive maturation is not triggered until a substantial portion of the ultimate body size has been achieved, as the mass at puberty represents roughly five percent of the estimated ultimate wet weight of 2391 grams [Wwi = 2391 grams] that can be attained by the largest adult specimens. This pattern of delayed maturation is common among zoarcids inhabiting cold, food-poor environments, where early investment in reproduction could compromise long-term survival and future fecundity.

Reproductive output in Lycodes eudipleurostictus appears to be constrained by the low ambient temperatures of its deep-water environment. Spawning adults produce demersal eggs that are deposited in protective nests, and despite the small size of individual offspring, the overall investment in reproduction can be considerable. Under the same thermal conditions that govern early development (3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of moderate fecundity per event and regular spawning intervals. Gravid females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with each clutch containing approximately 216 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 216 eggs]. This annual spawning frequency is typical of iteroparous zoarcids and ensures that energy reserves accumulated during the feeding season are incrementally allocated to gamete production rather than depleted in a single massive spawning event.

The maximum lifespan of the Doubleline eelpout has been estimated from otolith-based age readings of wild-caught individuals, with the oldest documented specimen reaching 13 years [am = 13 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]. This extended longevity, again measured at 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], is consistent with the species' slow growth and late maturation, forming part of a classic slow life-history syndrome that is widely observed among deep-sea benthic fishes. The combination of a lifespan exceeding a decade and a relatively late age at first reproduction suggests that only a few successful spawning events occur over an individual's lifetime, placing a premium on offspring survival and parental investment patterns. Comparative data from the congeneric Lycodes palearis indicate somewhat shorter lifespans, typically on the order of 10 to 12 years, which reinforces the view that L. eudipleurostictus occupies the slower end of the life-history continuum even within its own genus.
